lines.text: Start with the machine, not with syntax
A program can be perfectly written and still fail because the wrong Python executable is
running, the file was saved somewhere else, or the terminal is looking at a different folder. A
data engineer eventually runs code through schedulers and servers, so the habit starts now:
prove the runtime and prove the file you actually executed.
Before this lesson, all you need is the M00 computer/file foundation. No prior programming
knowledge is assumed.
Instructor demonstration: Luke Barousse - Python for Data Analytics, 00:08:42-00:18:52
(Getting Started). Watch the assigned range, then close the video and use this book. The
public title and chapter boundary were rechecked on 14 September 2026. The course book, not
the video, defines our evidence and failure exercise.
Picture what is happening
Think of a .py file as a written work order and the Python interpreter as the worker reading it
from top to bottom. The file is not "running" merely because it exists. When you type a
command such as:
py p01_first_program.py
you are asking a particular Python installation to open that particular file and execute its
statements. The terminal then shows standard output or an error/traceback. Those are
observations from a real run; the text in the editor is only the intended program.
New words you need now:

rows: A saved Python source file, usually ending .py
Normal text a program prints to the terminal
Grammar rules that make Python text parseable
Error report showing where Python failed and how execution reached that point
Folder the terminal currently treats as its starting location

lines.text: Follow with me once
Open a fresh terminal. First run:
py --version
Record the exact output. If py is unavailable but python --version works, record that instead;
do not pretend the commands are interchangeable on every PC.
Create a file named hello_m04.py containing:
print("Standalone DE 2026")
print(7 * 8)
Before running it, predict the output: one line of text and then 56. Now run the file from the
folder where it is saved:
py hello_m04.py
Expected output:
Standalone DE 2026
The multiplication happens before print displays the result. Nothing was stored automatically
in a spreadsheet or database; output exists only because the program printed it.
Now deliberately break the first line by removing the closing quote:
print("Standalone DE 2026)
Run again. Do not immediately repair it. Read the last part of the error. Python should report
a SyntaxError and point near the string that never closed. Save that failed terminal output.
Then repair the quote and rerun.
This tiny failure exercise matters because debugging begins with evidence. If you repair before
observing, you lose the chance to learn how Python describes failure.
What can go wrong on day one
If the terminal says the command is not recognized, the problem is not your print statement;
Python/launcher discovery failed. If Python says it cannot open the file, check the working
directory and filename. If a file named hello_m04.py.txt appears in Explorer, Windows may
have hidden the extension. If your editor "runs" a file but the terminal does something different,
write down the exact interpreter each environment uses rather than guessing.
A common beginner reaction is to reinstall everything. Avoid that. Isolate the boundary:
1. Can the terminal report a Python version?
2. Can the terminal show the folder containing your file?
3. Does the filename exactly match?
4. Can a two-line script run?
5. Only then investigate editor configuration.
Your independent attempt
Close the worked example. Create p01_first_program.py that prints your name, Standalone
DE 2026, and the result of 7 * 8. Then introduce a different syntax error from the one above,
save the traceback, diagnose it in one sentence, repair it and rerun from a fresh terminal.
Do not count "the green Run button worked once" as proof. Your evidence should include the
script, version command, first failure, repaired output and a short explanation of the edit -> run
-> observe -> repair loop.
Changed retry after review
If you needed the Explained Review, close it before retrying. Create another file that prints a
different label and calculates 9 * 6. Introduce another syntax error deliberately, explain the
final exception line before changing code, then repair it without reopening the review.
Ready-made revision
A Python source file is instructions; the interpreter executes them. Prove the interpreter with a
version command, prove the file/path you ran, read the last exception line before editing, and
preserve one failed attempt as debugging evidence.
A value that looks numeric may not be a number
Data engineering scripts carry many kinds of values at once: order IDs, quantities, prices,
booleans, timestamps and missing fields. Treating everything that contains digits as a number is
a classic way to destroy identifiers such as 0007 or attempt arithmetic on fields that should
never be averaged.
Instructor demonstration: Luke Barousse - Python for Data Analytics, 00:18:52-00:48:41
(Variables, Python terms and data types) in the same course. Close the video before the
independent task.
A variable is a name bound to an object/value. A type describes what kind of value Python is
dealing with and therefore which operations make sense. For this lesson, know these five:
Type
Example
Typical meaning
int
whole-number quantity/count
float
measurement/price with decimal
representation
str
text or identifier
bool
True
yes/no condition
NoneType
None
no Python value supplied
Assignment is not comparison
This line binds a name to a value:
qty = 4
This line asks a yes/no question:
qty == 4
The first uses = for assignment. The second uses == for equality comparison and returns a
boolean.
Follow with me once
Type this yourself:
order_id = "0007"
qty = 4
unit_price = 850.0
status = "Completed"
sales_rep = None
gross_sales = qty * unit_price
is_large = gross_sales >= 3000
print(order_id, type(order_id))
print(qty, type(qty))
print(unit_price, type(unit_price))
print(gross_sales, type(gross_sales))
print(is_large, type(is_large))
print(sales_rep, type(sales_rep))
Predict before running. order_id should remain text and keep its leading zeros. gross_sales
should be 3400.0, and is_large should be True.
Why does "0007" remain a string? Because its role is identity, not quantity. Turning it into
integer 7 would discard formatting and imply arithmetic meaning that the business field does
not have.
Now test a failure deliberately:
qty_text = "4"
print(qty_text * 3)
This does not produce 12. String multiplication repeats text, producing 444. Python is behaving
consistently with the type you gave it. If you actually received a quantity from text input and the
business contract says it must be an integer, parsing is a deliberate boundary decision:
qty_number = int(qty_text)
print(qty_number * 3)
Do not turn this into a habit of blindly calling int() on every digit-like field. First decide whether
the field is a measure or an identifier.
Arithmetic and comparisons
For beginner data work:
perform arithmetic, while:
produce booleans. A boolean can later control an if branch.
Be careful with floating-point equality. Binary floating-point cannot represent every decimal
fraction exactly. For monetary production systems you will later learn stronger numeric/decimal
choices. In this foundation lesson, don't build logic that assumes every calculated floating value
has a perfect decimal representation.
Independent task
Create:
order_id = O3107
qty = 4
unit_price = 850.0
status = Completed
using appropriate Python types. Calculate gross sales and a boolean for gross sales at least
3000. Print every value with type(...). Explain in your own words why order_id is text while
qty is numeric.
Validation is not "the script ran." Check that the numeric result is 3400.0, the threshold result is
true, the ID remains exactly O3107, and you can explain = versus == without notes.
Changed retry after review
Use shipment_id="S009", cartons=7, unit_cost=425.5, delivered=False. Calculate
shipment cost and:
needs_review = cost > 2500 and not delivered
Predict both outputs before running. Then explain why not delivered is meaningful only
because delivered is a boolean contract rather than a string such as "False".
Ready-made revision
Choose a Python type from business meaning, not appearance. IDs are often strings even when
they contain digits. = assigns; == compares. Arithmetic produces values; comparisons produce
booleans. Inspect type(value) before "fixing" a mysterious operation.
Text cleaning is not identity resolution
Source systems rarely send perfectly formatted labels. You may see " north HUB ", "North
Hub", and "NORTH HUB". Python can normalize those strings for comparison or display, but
formatting similarity does not prove that two records represent the same warehouse, customer
or product.
Instructor demonstration: Luke Barousse - Python for Data Analytics, 00:48:41-01:15:10
(Strings and string formatting). The video demonstrates Python string behavior; this book
adds data-provenance and cleaning boundaries.
A string is a sequence of Unicode characters. Strings are immutable: operations such as
.strip() and .lower() return new strings rather than editing the existing string in place.
Preserve raw and cleaned values separately
Start with:
raw_label = "  north HUB  "
clean_label = raw_label.strip().lower()
print(repr(raw_label))
print(repr(clean_label))
Expected:
'  north HUB  '
'north hub'
repr(...) is useful here because it makes surrounding spaces visible. If you printed the raw
value normally, you might miss the leading/trailing spaces with your eyes.
Why keep both? The raw value is provenance: what the source actually supplied. The cleaned
value is a transformation you chose. If the cleaning rule later proves too aggressive, the raw
value lets you reproduce and revise the transformation.
Useful operations, with their limits
text.strip()       # surrounding whitespace
text.lower()       # lowercase
text.upper()       # uppercase
text.replace(a,b)  # replace occurrences
text.startswith(x)
text.endswith(x)
text.split(sep)
sep.join(parts)
Do not read the comments as promises about business correctness. .replace(" ", "") can
remove meaningful spaces. .lower() can normalize case but cannot prove identity. split()
can parse a simple delimiter but is not a CSV parser when quoting/escaped delimiters matter.
Build a message with an f-string
An f-string makes values visible inside a human-readable string:
shipment_id = "S009"
cartons = 7
unit_cost = 425.5
cost = cartons * unit_cost
message = f"Shipment {shipment_id}: {cartons} cartons, cost={cost:.2f}"
print(message)
Expected cost is 2978.50. :.2f controls display formatting. It does not change the business
meaning of the original numeric value into "money-safe decimal arithmetic"; it only controls how
this value is formatted in the string.
Indexing and slicing: useful, but don't infer contracts from samples
Python strings can be indexed and sliced:
code = "WH-EAST-007"
print(code[0:2])
print(code[-3:])
You might get WH and 007. That does not mean all future IDs are guaranteed to have the same
shape. Before slicing production identifiers, obtain or define the source contract.
Deliberate collision example
Run:
raw_values = [" Pen ", "PEN", "pen", "Pen Blue"]
for value in raw_values:
print(repr(value), "->", value.strip().lower())
Three values collapse to pen; one becomes pen blue. If the first three are known variants of the
same product label, that may be useful. If they are case-sensitive external keys, collapsing them
would be corruption. Cleaning is a rule, not a universal truth.
Independent task
Start with:
raw_label = "  NORTH Hub  "
shipment_id = "s009"
Keep the raw label. Create a cleaned display label using deliberate .strip() and case
normalization. Create an uppercase display form of the shipment ID without overwriting the
original. Build an f-string explaining raw -> cleaned values. Then demonstrate one pair of strings
that look similar after formatting but should not automatically be treated as the same identity.
Validate by printing repr(raw_label), the cleaned value and the message. Explain why a
formatted value can be useful for display while an authoritative key should come from the data
contract.
Changed retry after review
Given " Pen Blue ", "pen blue" (two internal spaces) and "PEN BLUE", normalize only
surrounding spaces and case. Compare results. Do not silently collapse internal spaces. Explain
what additional business rule would be needed before deciding those labels are equivalent.
Ready-made revision
Strings are immutable. Preserve raw text, create cleaned/display values separately, and use
repr() when invisible whitespace matters. An f-string formats a message; formatting is not
identity proof. Never turn "looks similar" into "same entity" without a declared rule.
Business rules become branches
A pipeline repeatedly asks questions: Is the record valid? Is the file late? Is the order eligible?
Should this row go to quarantine? Python conditions are how written business rules become
executable decisions.
Instructor demonstration: Luke Barousse - Python for Data Analytics, 01:26:20-01:34:24
(Conditional Statements). Our lesson adds boundary testing and rule validation.
A condition is an expression interpreted as true or false. if, elif and else choose which block
executes. Indentation is part of Python syntax: it marks which statements belong to the branch.
Translate the English sentence first
Business rule:
> An order is priority only when its status is Completed and its amount is at least 2500.
Write the logic before the code:
status == Completed
AND
amount >= 2500
Then Python:
status = "Completed"
amount = 2500
if status == "Completed" and amount >= 2500:
label = "priority"
else:
label = "standard"
print(label)
At exactly 2500 the label should be priority because the rule says at least, meaning >= rather
than >.
Prove the boundary, not only a comfortable example
Use this test table before running:
Run all four. The exact boundary is often where real defects hide. One happy-path test cannot
prove >= was implemented correctly.
and, or, not
and requires both conditions. or accepts at least one. not reverses a boolean.
Consider:
status == "Completed" or amount >= 2500
That would incorrectly label Pending/3000 as priority. The code can run perfectly and still
implement the wrong policy.
When rules mix and and or, use parentheses to make intent visible rather than relying on
remembered precedence:
eligible = (region == "East" or region == "West") and status == "Completed"
Missingness is not the same as false
Suppose delivered may be True, False or None. None means "no value supplied," not
automatically "not delivered." A rule such as:
if not delivered:
would treat both False and None as falsy. That may be wrong if unknown delivery status must
be quarantined separately. Prefer explicit contracts:
if delivered is True:
state = "delivered"
elif delivered is False:
state = "not_delivered"
else:
state = "unknown"
This is your first glimpse of a recurring engineering principle: unknown is not automatically
zero/false/no.
Recovery ladder
If a condition behaves unexpectedly:
1. Rewrite the business rule in one sentence.
2. Split it into individual booleans.
3. Print each boolean separately.
4. Test below / exactly at / above every numeric boundary.
5. Include a disqualifying case.
6. Only then combine the expression.
Independent task
Implement the priority rule above from a blank file and test all four boundary cases. Save
predictions before execution. Add one explicit None example for a boolean-like field and explain
why unknown should not automatically equal false.
Changed retry after review
A shipment is escalate only when delayed_days >= 2 and priority_customer is True. Test
1, 2 and 3 delayed days for both customer flags, plus one priority_customer=None case. State
what your code does with unknown priority and why.
Ready-made revision
Write the English rule first. and means all required conditions; or means at least one;
parentheses make mixed rules auditable. Test boundaries and disqualifying cases. None can
mean unknown and should not be silently treated as a business False unless the contract says
so.
Four containers, four different promises
Python gives you several built-in collection types. Beginners often learn them as syntax to
memorize; an engineer chooses them based on the promise the program needs: preserve
sequence, keep a fixed grouping, enforce uniqueness/membership, or map a key to a value.
Instructor demonstration: Luke Barousse - Python for Data Analytics, 01:34:24-02:12:26
(Lists, dictionaries, sets and tuples). Watch the demonstrations, then return here to choose
by engineering requirement rather than visual preference.
Picture four containers:
• a list is an ordered tray whose contents can change;
• a tuple is an ordered grouping commonly used when the grouping should be treated as fixed;
• a set is a membership collection that keeps unique hashable values and does not promise
list-style positional order;
• a dictionary maps unique keys to values.
Start with the requirement, then choose
pipeline_steps = ["extract", "validate", "publish"]
period = (2026, 9)
failed_batch_ids = {"B17", "B22", "B17"}
region_manager = {"East": "Asha", "West": "Om"}
print(pipeline_steps)
print(period)
print(failed_batch_ids)
print(region_manager["East"])
pipeline_steps is a list because sequence matters and we may add/remove a step. period is a
tuple because year/month belong together and we do not need in-place edits. The set keeps B17
once because membership/uniqueness is the purpose. The dict lets us retrieve a manager by
region key.
Mutation matters
Lists and dictionaries are mutable. That means this:
steps = ["extract", "load"]
other_name = steps
other_name.append("validate")
print(steps)
prints a list that now includes validate. other_name did not create an independent copy; both
names refer to the same list object.
For a shallow copy of a flat list:
copied = steps.copy()
creates another outer list. Later you will learn that nested mutable objects make copying more
subtle; do not build a false rule that .copy() recursively duplicates everything.
This distinction matters in pipelines because one helper can unexpectedly mutate data another
part of the program still expects to be unchanged.
Sets solve membership problems, not ordering problems
seen = set()
for order_id in ["O1", "O2", "O1"]:
if order_id in seen:
print("duplicate candidate:", order_id)
else:
seen.add(order_id)
The set is useful because we care whether an ID has appeared, not where it appears by index. A
set can be faster for repeated membership checks than scanning a list; DE04-12 explains that
growth intuition.
But if first-occurrence order matters, a set alone is insufficient. One common pattern is a set for
membership plus a list for ordered output:
seen = set()
unique_in_order = []
for order_id in ["O2", "O1", "O2", "O3"]:
if order_id not in seen:
seen.add(order_id)
unique_in_order.append(order_id)
Dictionary keys are an identity contract
A dict cannot hold two simultaneous values under the same key in the same mapping. Assigning
the key again replaces the previous value:
manager = {"East": "Asha"}
manager["East"] = "Ravi"
That is not a duplicate-record store. If multiple managers per region are valid, the value itself
could be a list, or you may need a different data model. The collection should match the
relationship.
Use .get() when absence is expected and you have consciously chosen how to represent it:
print(manager.get("North"))       # None
print(manager.get("North", "Unknown"))
Be careful: the display label Unknown is your added fallback. It is not a region supplied by the
source.
Independent task
Represent four requirements:
1. three processing steps that must keep order;
2. a fixed (year, month) reporting period;
3. failed batch IDs where duplicates should collapse;
4. a region-to-manager lookup.
Print and manipulate each structure enough to prove its behavior. Then create a list, assign a
second name to it, mutate through the second name, and explain why the original changed.
Create a separate copy and prove the outer list is independent.
Changed retry after review
Represent warehouse zones and supervisors, a unique set of failed shipment IDs, a processing
sequence, and a fixed (country_code, year) pair. Add a case where one zone legitimately has
two supervisors and redesign the dictionary value rather than silently overwriting one name.
Ready-made revision
List = ordered mutable sequence. Tuple = ordered fixed-style grouping. Set = unique
membership. Dict = key -> value lookup. Choose by the requirement, not by whichever syntax
you remember. Assignment can create two names for the same mutable object; copying
behavior must be deliberate.
Repetition should make work clearer, not hide repeated mistakes
A data pipeline applies logic to many records. Loops let you express "for each item" without
copy-pasting the same statements. The risk is equally important: if the logic is wrong, a loop
repeats the wrong action consistently across the dataset.
Instructor demonstration: Luke Barousse - Python for Data Analytics, 02:21:06-02:44:16
(Loops and list-comprehension lead-in). The course uses explicit loops first because they
make state changes visible.
An iterable is an object you can step through. An iteration is one pass through the loop body.
An accumulator is a value updated across iterations, such as a running total. break exits a loop
early; continue skips to the next iteration.
Follow one record at a time
total = 0
positive_count = 0
invalid = []
for amount in amounts:
if amount <= 0:
invalid.append(amount)
continue
total += amount
positive_count += 1
print(total)
print(positive_count)
print(invalid)
Predict first. Positive total should be 4000, positive count 4, invalid list [0].
The source list is unchanged. We created result state separately. That is a useful default habit:
do not mutate the collection you are currently iterating over unless you can prove the behavior
you want.
Why mutating while iterating can surprise you
for value in values:
if value == 0:
values.remove(value)
print(values)
A beginner may expect [1, 2], but removing elements shifts positions while the iterator
advances. One zero can be skipped. Prefer a new collection:
clean = [value for value in values if value != 0]
or an explicit loop appending accepted values. The important principle is not "list
comprehensions are always better"; it is do not make source mutation an accidental side
effect of traversal.
range and enumerate
Use range when you genuinely need a sequence of integers. Use enumerate when you need
both position and value:
steps = ["extract", "validate", "publish"]
for position, step in enumerate(steps, start=1):
print(position, step)
Do not use indexes merely because you learned them first. for row in rows: is usually clearer
than for i in range(len(rows)): when you only need each row.
Loop over dictionaries deliberately
regional_sales = {"East": 11700, "West": 8100}
for region, sales in regional_sales.items():
print(region, sales)
.items() makes key and value explicit. Iterating directly over the dict yields keys. Neither is
"the right way" universally; choose the shape your loop needs.
Nested loops and cost intuition
If every left record scans every right record, work grows quickly:
for order in orders:
for customer in customers:
You do not need full algorithm analysis yet, but notice the pattern. DE04-12 will connect it to
O(n²)-style growth and lookup structures.
Independent task
Using amounts=[1200,500,0,800,1500], calculate positive total/count and collect invalid
non-positive values without changing the original list. Prove the original input is unchanged.
Then iterate a dictionary of three regional totals and print a numbered report using enumerate
over a deliberately ordered list of regions.
Add a test with an empty amounts=[]. Decide what total/count should be and prove your code
handles it without a special crash.
Changed retry after review
Given shipment weights [12.5, -1, 0, 8.0, 15.2], create accepted and rejected lists, total
only positive weights, and leave the source list intact. Explain why removing bad values from
the same list during iteration is a weaker design.
Ready-made revision
A loop repeats a block for each item. Keep input and result state separate when possible. Use
continue to skip a record deliberately, break only when early termination is truly the
requirement, enumerate for position + value, and .items() for dict key/value pairs. Do not
casually mutate the collection you are traversing.
A pipeline is easier to trust when logic has named boundaries
Copy-pasted calculations are hard to test and easy to let drift. A function gives a name to a
piece of behavior, defines what inputs it receives and what output it returns. Later modules will
build ingestion and transformation pipelines from functions, so the key habit is to make
dependencies visible.
Instructor demonstration: Luke Barousse - Python for Data Analytics, 02:52:12-03:12:46
(Functions; lambda is optional context). Focus on function definition/calls/return values.
Lambda syntax is not a mastery requirement here.
New words:
• function: reusable block of behavior called by name;
• parameter: name in the function definition;
• argument: actual value supplied in a call;
• return value: value sent back to the caller;
• local variable: name created inside the function's local scope;
• scope: rules determining where a name can be accessed;
• pure-ish function: informal term here for a function whose result mostly depends on explicit
inputs and avoids hidden side effects.
Follow with me once
def summarize_order(order_id, qty, unit_price):
gross_sales = qty * unit_price
return {
"order_id": order_id,
"gross_sales": gross_sales,
first = summarize_order("O1", 2, 850.0)
second = summarize_order("O2", 3, 500.0)
print(first)
print(second)
Expected gross values are 1700.0 and 1500.0. The function does not know about a global qty; it
receives all three required values through parameters.
print is not return
This function:
def show_total(qty, unit_price):
print(qty * unit_price)
displays a value but implicitly returns None. If later code needs the number for validation,
filtering or aggregation, printing is not enough.
def calculate_total(qty, unit_price):
return qty * unit_price
Now the caller can store, test or combine the result.
Hidden global state makes behavior harder to reason about
tax_rate = 0.18
def total_with_tax(amount):
return amount * (1 + tax_rate)
This can work, but the function depends on a name not visible in its signature. If tax_rate
changes elsewhere, the same call may produce a different answer. Configuration globals are
sometimes legitimate, but understand the dependency. For a beginner exercise, explicit input is
clearer:
def total_with_tax(amount, tax_rate):
return amount * (1 + tax_rate)
Default arguments and mutable defaults
A safe simple default:
def label_order(order_id, prefix="ORDER"):
return f"{prefix}:{order_id}"
A classic pitfall:
def add_error(message, errors=[]):
errors.append(message)
return errors
That list is created once when the function is defined and reused across calls. Prefer:
def add_error(message, errors=None):
if errors is None:
errors = []
errors.append(message)
return errors
You do not need to memorize every Python function nuance now; you do need to learn that
hidden shared mutable state can leak across calls.
Validate functions with multiple inputs
One successful call proves little. For summarize_order, try:
• normal positive quantity;
• zero quantity;
• another price;
• later, an invalid type to see the failure boundary.
A function contract should state what valid inputs mean and what output shape it returns.
Independent task
Write summarize_order(order_id, qty, unit_price) returning a dict with order_id and
gross_sales. Test two normal inputs and one zero-quantity input. Show that the returned dict
can be assigned and reused. Then write a deliberately weak version that prints but returns
nothing, inspect its actual return with print(type(result)), and explain the difference.
Changed retry after review
Write shipment_cost(shipment_id, cartons, cost_per_carton) returning a dict with ID and
cost. Test three cases including zero cartons. Then extend it to accept an explicit currency
argument rather than reading a hidden global. Explain which inputs are measures and which are
identifiers/labels.
Ready-made revision
Functions create named behavior boundaries. Parameters make dependencies visible;
arguments are supplied values; return gives a result to the caller. Printing is observation, not a
reusable return value. Avoid hidden mutable state and test more than one input.
One file is useful until it becomes one giant file
As programs grow, keeping every helper and every execution step in one script becomes
difficult to navigate and test. A Python module is simply a Python file that can be imported. The
key beginner lesson is not "make lots of folders"; it is to separate reusable logic from the code
that starts a run, while understanding that importing a module executes its top-level statements
once per interpreter process.
Instructor demonstration: Luke Barousse - Python for Data Analytics, 03:12:46-03:40:05
(Modules and Python library lead-in). Our book adds import side-effect and entry-point
reasoning.
Use the supplied practice/stage04_helpers.py:
def gross_sales(qty, unit_price):
return qty * unit_price
def normalized_label(text):
return text.strip().lower()
Create a separate run_order.py in your working folder:
from stage04_helpers import gross_sales, normalized_label
def main():
amount = gross_sales(3, 500.0)
label = normalized_label("  EAST HUB ")
print(label, amount)
if __name__ == "__main__":
main()
Expected output is east hub 1500.0.
What __name__ is protecting
When a file is run directly, Python sets its __name__ to "__main__". When it is imported,
__name__ is the module name. Therefore the guard:
if __name__ == "__main__":
main()
lets you keep "start the program" behavior separate from "make functions available for import."
Deliberately add this line at the top level of the helper file:
print("helper imported")
Then run run_order.py. You will see the message during import. That proves top-level module
code executes as part of import. Remove the diagnostic after understanding it. A module should
not unexpectedly start a data pipeline merely because another file imported one helper.
Import styles
import stage04_helpers
stage04_helpers.gross_sales(2, 850)
makes the module name explicit.
from stage04_helpers import gross_sales
gross_sales(2, 850)
is shorter. Both are valid. Avoid wildcard imports such as from module import * in our course
because they hide which names entered the current namespace.
Name collisions and shadowing
Do not name your learner file pandas.py, csv.py, json.py or pathlib.py when you intend to
import the standard/library package of that name. Python can find your local file first and import

OPTIONAL visual - no verified bounded range.
An exception is an object representing a runtime error condition. A traceback shows the chain
of calls that led to an unhandled exception. try marks code that may raise an expected
exception; except handles a selected exception type. else can run when no exception
occurred; finally runs whether the try succeeded or failed, commonly for cleanup.
Read the traceback from the bottom first
Open a copy of practice/M04_Debug_Me.py. It contains records with deliberately inconsistent
values. Run it without editing. Save the full traceback.
A traceback often contains several file/line frames, but the final line normally tells you the
exception class and message. For example:
TypeError: can't multiply sequence by non-int of type 'float'
Do not search the entire internet for that sentence before checking the values at the failing
expression. Add temporary observations:
print(order)
print(type(order["qty"]), type(order["unit_price"]))
The purpose is to identify the first broken assumption. In the starter file, one quantity is text.
The safe repair depends on the contract: if the input specification says quantity must be an
integer represented as text, parse and validate it; if arbitrary text is allowed, the calculation
itself may not be valid.
Catch narrowly, not broadly
A dangerous beginner pattern is:
try:
except Exception:
pass
This hides every ordinary exception and throws away the reason. The program may then
continue with partial or wrong output.
A more deliberate boundary might be:
raw_qty = "3"
try:
qty = int(raw_qty)
except ValueError as exc:
print(f"invalid quantity: {raw_qty!r}")
raise
Here we expect int(...) can raise ValueError for non-integer text. We log context and
re-raise because this beginner script has no approved quarantine policy yet. Later modules will
build rejected-row handling.
Exceptions are not a substitute for validation
If the business contract requires qty > 0, successful int("0") parsing does not make zero
valid. Type conversion answers "can Python represent this as an integer?" Business validation
answers "is this value allowed for this field?" Keep those questions separate.
Deliberate division failure
Consider:
sales = 0.0
qty = 0
average_unit = sales / qty
This raises ZeroDivisionError. Catching it and returning zero would invent a meaning unless
the business contract explicitly defines an average for zero quantity. Sometimes the right
behavior is to reject/flag the record, not force a numeric answer.
Debug one cause at a time
Use this order:
1. Reproduce the failure.
2. Save exact input and traceback.
3. Read the final exception type/message.
4. Find the earliest line where an assumption becomes false.
5. Add the smallest diagnostic observation.
6. Repair one cause.
7. Rerun the same case.
8. Remove temporary debug prints or convert them into deliberate logging later.
9. Add a test that would catch the failure if it returns.
Changing five lines at once destroys evidence about which change fixed the problem.

Data engineering crosses boundaries between memory and files
So far most values disappeared when the script ended. Real pipelines read files, validate them
and write outputs another process can consume. File I/O introduces new failure boundaries:
path, encoding, file format, schema and serialization.

New words:
• path: location of a file/folder;
• relative path: location interpreted from a known base rather than a machine-specific
absolute drive path;
• encoding: mapping between characters and bytes; use UTF-8 explicitly in our text files;
• serialization: converting an in-memory structure to a storable/transmittable representation
such as JSON;
• schema: expected fields/types/meaning;
• read-back validation: reopening what you wrote and checking it rather than trusting the
write call.

Read CSV with the standard library
import csv
with orders_path.open("r", encoding="utf-8", newline="") as handle:
reader = csv.DictReader(handle)
rows = list(reader)
print(reader.fieldnames)
print(len(rows))

not make it an integer. Parsing belongs at the boundary with explicit error handling.
Do not use line.split(',') as a replacement CSV parser. Quoted commas and escaping rules
make CSV more than "text separated by commas."
Validate schema before doing calculations
required = {"order_id", "region", "status", "qty", "unit_price", "sales_rep"}
actual = set(reader.fieldnames or [])
missing = required - actual
if missing:
raise ValueError(f"missing required columns: {sorted(missing)}")

missing-key error halfway through the pipeline.
JSON preserves structure, not arbitrary Python objects
import json
manifest = {
"source": orders_path.name,
"expected_rows": len(rows),
"status": "training",
manifest_path = HERE / "run_manifest.json"
with manifest_path.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
json.dump(manifest, handle, indent=2, sort_keys=True)
with manifest_path.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
loaded = json.load(handle)
assert loaded == manifest

directly JSON serializable; standard JSON values are objects/maps, arrays, strings, numbers,
booleans and null. A Path or datetime typically needs explicit conversion to a serializable
representation.

Think about growth before data becomes large
A script can be correct on five rows and painfully slow on five million. Big-O notation gives a
rough language for how work grows with input size. It does not predict exact seconds and it
does not replace measurement/profiling.
Instructor demonstration: freeCodeCamp - Data Structures and Algorithms in Python,
00:50:52-01:24:57 (Complexity and Big O notation). This is the complete bounded Big-O
chapter used by M04; stop at the Binary Search vs Linear Search chapter boundary. We are not
turning M04 into a competitive-programming course.
The four growth ideas you need now
• O(1): roughly constant work independent of collection size for the operation considered;
• O(n): work grows proportionally with the number of items;
• O(n log n): common comparison-sort growth class;
• O(n²): quadratic growth, often from a full nested scan.
Big-O ignores constant factors and lower-order terms to focus on scaling behavior. 3n + 10 is
O(n), not because 3 and 10 do not cost time, but because linear growth dominates as n gets
large.
Repeated membership: list versus set
ids_list = ["A", "B", "C", "D"]
ids_set = set(ids_list)
print("C" in ids_list)
print("C" in ids_set)
A list membership check may scan values until a match is found, so worst-case growth is O(n).
Set membership is average O(1) because sets use hashing, while acknowledging
pathological/worst-case implementation details are more complex than this foundation model.
Now imagine checking 100,000 incoming IDs against 100,000 known IDs. Repeated list scans
can approach a nested-work pattern; building a set once can turn the repeated membership
operation into far cheaper average lookup.
Nested scan
for order in orders:
for customer in customers:
if order["customer_id"] == customer["customer_id"]:
If both collections grow around n and each order scans every customer, comparisons grow
roughly n x n = n². A dictionary keyed by customer ID can convert the repeated lookup into
average O(1) after one O(n)-style build pass.
This is the same engineering instinct you used in SQL joins: identity/key structure matters.
Sorting is not free
Python's built-in sorting is highly optimized and generally has O(n log n) comparison-based
behavior. That does not mean you should write your own sorting algorithm for production. The
lesson is to recognize that sorting large datasets costs more than one simple scan and should
serve a clear requirement.
Don't misuse micro-benchmarks
Timing four values once and seeing a set slower than a list does not disprove the growth model.
Creating the set itself has cost; cache effects and tiny constants dominate small inputs. Big-O
asks how the algorithm's work grows, while profiling asks how this implementation performs
under realistic conditions. You will use both ideas later.

Guided pattern: reverse word order
Requirement: given a string, return the words in reverse order while preserving characters
inside each word.
For:
data engineering is fun
expected:
fun is engineering data
One clear implementation:
def reverse_words(text):
words = text.split()
words.reverse()
return " ".join(words)
Trace it:
"data engineering is fun"
-> ["data", "engineering", "is", "fun"]
-> ["fun", "is", "engineering", "data"]
-> "fun is engineering data"
For blank input, split() returns an empty list and joining it returns an empty string. That is a
useful edge case to test.
There are alternative valid implementations, such as slicing words[::-1]. Mastery is not
matching one preferred line. You should be able to state the contract, predict output and defend
why your code satisfies it.

def count_vowels(text):

Use a mapping when the problem is about counts or lookup
Dictionaries and sets are especially useful in coding screens because they let you express

Frequency map
Requirement: count occurrences of each item while preserving the item as the dictionary key.
def frequency_map(items):
counts = {}
for item in items:
counts[item] = counts.get(item, 0) + 1
return counts
For:
expect:
Trace A: absent -> default 0 -> 1; later 1 -> 2; later 2 -> 3. The dictionary is storing one
aggregate state per key.
Do not confuse this with source-grain preservation. Once you turn five events into three
dictionary keys, you have aggregated occurrences by item. If each occurrence needs separate
metadata, a simple frequency dictionary is no longer the whole data model.
Unique values while preserving first occurrence order
A set alone gives membership but not the list-style "first occurrence order" result contract.
Combine structures:
def unique_in_order(items):
seen = set()
result = []
for item in items:
if item not in seen:
seen.add(item)
result.append(item)
return result
For:
B, A, B, C, A
expect:
B, A, C
The set answers "seen?" efficiently; the list preserves output order.
Missing key versus key mapped to missing value
These are different states:
record = {"sales_rep": None}
print("sales_rep" in record)       # True
print(record.get("sales_rep"))     # None
print(record.get("manager"))       # None
Both .get(...) calls return None, but one key exists with a missing value and the other key
does not exist. If that distinction matters, test membership explicitly:
if "manager" not in record:
Do not let convenience methods erase the difference between "field absent" and "field present
but unknown."

A tuple can be used as a dictionary/set key when identity requires multiple fields:
seen = set()
seen.add(key)
This mirrors the composite-key thinking from SQL: (order_id, line_no) can identify an order

Stack: last in, first out
Picture trays stacked on top of each other. The last tray placed is the first removed.
stack = []
stack.append("extract")
stack.append("transform")
stack.append("load")
last = stack.pop()
print(last)
print(stack)
Expected last is load; remaining stack is extract, transform.
Stacks show up in undo-style reasoning, nested parsing and traversal. You do not need to force
a stack into ordinary pipeline scheduling just because you learned it.
Queue: first in, first out
Use collections.deque for efficient operations at both ends:
from collections import deque
queue = deque()
queue.append("job-1")
queue.append("job-2")
first = queue.popleft()
print(first)
Expected first item is job-1. A queue models work processed in arrival order when FIFO is the
actual contract.
Linear search
def linear_search(values, target):
for index, value in enumerate(values):
if value == target:
return index
return -1
This works on arbitrary order. Worst-case it inspects all n values -> O(n).
Binary search requires sorted input
Binary search repeatedly discards half of a sorted search interval. If the input is unsorted, the
elimination logic is invalid.
def binary_search(values, target):
low = 0
high = len(values) - 1
while low <= high:
mid = (low + high) // 2
if values[mid] == target:
return mid
if values[mid] < target:
low = mid + 1
else:
high = mid - 1
return -1
For sorted input, search growth is O(log n). But if you must sort fresh unsorted data just once
solely to search one target, sorting cost can dominate. Algorithm choice depends on the broader
workflow, not only lookup complexity.
sorted() versus .sort()
new_values = sorted(values)
print(values)
print(new_values)
sorted(values) returns a new list and leaves the original unchanged.
values.sort()
sorts the list in place and returns None. If source order is meaningful evidence, copying/sorted
output may be safer. If mutating the working list is intended, .sort() can be appropriate. State
which contract you need.

Your input contract
For data/M04_Retail_Orders.csv, required columns are:
order_id, region, status, qty, unit_price, sales_rep
One source row represents one order in this training fixture. order_id must be unique. qty and
unit_price must be parseable numeric values appropriate for the calculation. Do not silently
replace malformed values with zero. Raw input remains unchanged.
Your output contract
Produce one deterministic JSON document containing at least:
• source filename;
• source row count;
• Completed row count;
• Completed sales total;
• regional Completed totals;
• top 3 Completed orders under a declared deterministic sort;
• missing sales_rep count over a clearly named population.
Stable output means the same valid input and code produce the same logical structure and
ordering. Use a deliberate sort order for dictionaries/lists that otherwise depend on source order
or equal values. json.dump(..., sort_keys=True, indent=2) helps stable text formatting but
does not by itself define how your top-3 list handles ties; you must define that in the data logic.
Validation must challenge a plausible wrong result
At minimum prove:
• input rows = 25;
• Completed rows = 23;
• Completed sales = 39320;
• regional Completed totals reconcile to 39320;
• one missing sales rep is visible under the chosen population;
• top-3 order IDs/values satisfy your sort rule;
• raw CSV hash/content is not modified by your program;
• output JSON can be read back and critical values match what was calculated.
Do not paste these numbers into the output as constants. They are controls to compare against
the values your pipeline calculates.
Deliberate failure proof
Run the program with data/M04_Bad_Orders.csv. The supplied bad file lacks required qty. Your
checkpoint should fail at the schema boundary with a clear message rather than stumbling later
into a KeyError or fabricated calculation.
Also test a missing file path. Those are two different failure boundaries: path existence versus
schema contract.
Reproducibility evidence
Write an exact command such as:
py M04_Checkpoint_TODO.py
or whatever explicit argument form you designed. Close/reopen the terminal and prove the
documented command still works from the location you documented. Another learner should
not need your personal desktop path or editor button.
Your evidence bundle should include first attempt, observed controls, output JSON, one
bad-input failure, run command/transcript and a short architecture explanation.

Ready-made revision
A reproducible script has an explicit entry point, input contract, validation boundaries,
deterministic output and documented run command. Validate before transformation, preserve
raw input, reconcile important totals, prove a failure path and read outputs back. "It ran on my
laptop" is not the same as reproducible engineering.
